title: F_d(n): Minimum Guaranteed Distinct-Distance Subset
content: The quantity F_d(n) is defined as: the minimum, over all n-point configurations P in ℝ^d, of the maximum size of a subset S ⊆ P such that all pairwise distances in S are distinct. This is a min-max quantity: the 'min' is over adversarial configurations, the 'max' is the best distinct-distance subset we can extract. So F_d(n) is the size of distinct-distance subset guaranteed to exist regardless of how the n points are placed.
mathContext: $F_d(n) = \min_{|P|=n, P \subset \mathbb{R}^d} \max\{|S| : S \subseteq P, \text{ all } \binom{|S|}{2} \text{ distances distinct}\}$.

title: Greedy Lower Bound: F_d(n) ≥ Ω(√n)
content: A greedy algorithm gives F_d(n) ≥ ⌊√n⌋. Build S greedily: start with any point, repeatedly add a point p such that the distances from p to all current points in S are distinct from all existing pairwise distances in S. At step k (when |S| = k), the number of 'forbidden' distance values from p is at most k(k-1)/2 (existing pairwise distances in S). Since P has n - k remaining candidate points, as long as n - k > k(k-1)/2 we can find p. This gives k = Ω(n^{1/2}).
mathContext: At step $k$: $|S| = k$, existing distances = $\binom{k}{2}$. We need a new point avoiding $\le k-1$ bad distances (each matching one of the $\binom{k}{2}$ values). By pigeonhole: if $n - k > k-1$ we can continue. The algorithm stops when $k \approx \sqrt{n}$.

title: Connection to Guth-Katz Distinct Distances (d=2)
content: For d=2, the problem is closely related to the Guth-Katz theorem (2015): any n points in the plane determine Ω(n/log n) distinct distances. The connection is: if P determines D distinct distances, then a largest distinct-distance subset S of P has |S| related to D. If D = Ω(n/log n), then F_2(n) ≥ Ω((n/log n)^{1/2}). The problem is listed as solved, suggesting tight bounds are known for all d, possibly using polynomial method or incidence geometry techniques from Guth-Katz.
mathContext: Guth-Katz (2015): any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determine $\ge cn/\log n$ distinct distances. For $d=2$, Erdős conjectured $F_2(n) = \Theta(n^{2/3})$ (related to the number of distinct distances from a single point in certain configurations).

title: Dimension Dependence and the d ≥ 2 Condition
content: The problem specifies d ≥ 2 (the planar and higher-dimensional case). For d = 1 (points on a line), any configuration can be perturbed to have all distances distinct, so F_1(n) = n trivially. The interesting case is d = 2 where points can be placed on structured sets (circle, grid) that limit distinct-distance subsets. For large d, the 'curse of dimensionality' means fewer distance coincidences, and F_d(n) likely grows faster with d.
mathContext: In $\mathbb{R}^1$: generic $n$ points have all $\binom{n}{2}$ distances distinct, so $F_1(n) = n$. In $\mathbb{R}^2$: a regular $n$-gon has each distance value appearing $n$ times, forcing $F_2(n) \le O(n^{2/3})$. The problem asks for the tight asymptotics for each $d \ge 2$.
